It hasn't disappeared but the technology has shifted where it is applied. When the graphics, sound and controls were simple a lot of craftmanship went into other things such as interactivity, game genre etc, level tuning, overall game length. The amount of game hours required to create a map was small so more time was devoted to tuning how a level played. It also meant there was a lot more content (from a game play time perspective) for the player to explore. More modern games have a miraculous level realism with incredibly detailed environments and characters. Craftmanship goes into making a character look life-like and animate in an incredibly believable way. This take thousands of man hours and tuning to get it right. This is where you find craftmanship. There is a downside though because teams are now upwards of 100 people working over multiyears in order to have a reasonable amount of game play. This has raised the costs of production several hundred fold from the dawn of video game production. Consequently, the publishers have become much more conservative in what titles get backed and is the main reason for sequelitus.
